intro_band.agent_remit_summary: The AutoGen Code Executor is the component of a multi-agent workflow that takes code blocks produced by a coder or orchestrator agent, runs them inside a controlled execution environment, and returns the exit code and captured output. The remit authorizes containerized execution on a Docker backend and remote sandboxed Python on Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions, plus file upload/download, session restart and container lifecycle management, reached only over the agent runtime message bus, the Docker daemon, and the configured ACA pool endpoint. A sandboxed backend is required for all execution; the local host executor may be used only with explicit operator authorization in a trusted, non-production context. Human confirmation is required before every code-block execution with no risk-threshold carve-out, and if the sandbox backend is unavailable the executor must halt and alert the operator rather than fall back to unsandboxed host execution.
intro_band.agent_structure_summary: Python, part of the AutoGen monorepo: an abstract CodeExecutor in autogen-core/code_executor/_base.py plus five concrete backends in autogen-ext/code_executors/ — local command line, Docker command line, Docker-hosted Jupyter kernel gateway, host-local Jupyter (nbclient), and Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions — sharing helpers in _common.py. Each backend writes a code block to a file in a working directory and runs it in a fresh process, container exec, or kernel cell; create_default_code_executor() selects Docker when reachable and otherwise returns the host-local executor. External surfaces include the Docker daemon socket, container image registries, a published Jupyter kernel-gateway HTTP/WebSocket port, and the ACA pool-management endpoint reached with a bearer token. No approval or confirmation logic exists anywhere in the executor packages — the only gate is an optional approval_func parameter on CodeExecutorAgent in the caller package, which defaults to None.

behavior_summary: The dominant pattern is a sandbox with the shape of isolation but not the substance: the isolation boundary is real when Docker is chosen, but every path around it is unguarded and several downgrade silently. create_default_code_executor() answers an unreachable Docker daemon with a warnings.warn and a host-local executor rather than the halt-and-alert the remit requires, the LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor docstring advertises a regex sanitizer against dangerous commands that exists nowhere in the code, and the bundled Jupyter kernel gateway binds 0.0.0.0 with publish_all_ports=True over cleartext WebSocket. Underneath that sits the Step-7 chain a security lead should read first: code blocks arrive with no provenance check, no confirmation gate is active by default, and the resulting process inherits the full host environment — untrusted content to host execution in one hop. Even on the intended Docker path the container is created with no network, user, capability, or resource restrictions, and no backend records what it executed.

rules.rule_text: The executor MUST NOT execute code, or act on execution instructions, that originate from untrusted retrieved content, tool output, or web/document data; it runs only code blocks delivered through the authorized agent workflow.

The executor MUST NOT autonomously perform irreversible real-world actions on the basis of generated output (for example publishing or posting content, or sending external communications) — a human decides how execution outputs are used.
The executor MUST NOT expand or redefine its own role beyond executing supplied code blocks and returning their results; it does not set its own goals or acquire capabilities on its own initiative.
The executor MUST NOT be operated as an unattended, production-facing service without the additional safety evaluation, hardening, and human oversight its deployment requires.
Approved Communication Channels
Trusted People / Accounts
Trusted Services / Integrations

Only the operator-configured ACA pool-management endpoint / credential provider and the approved Docker daemon target are authorized backend endpoints; any other backend endpoint, daemon target, or credential/token provider is a trust-expansion finding.
Arbitrary external network endpoints, third-party services, or MCP servers that are not required to execute the supplied code within the authorized backend.
Allowed Tools (Known Good Baseline)
A sandboxed execution backend (Docker or Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions) is required for all code execution.

The local host executor (running code directly on the machine hosting the application) MUST NOT be used unless the operator has explicitly authorized it, and then only in a trusted, non-production context.
The executor MUST NOT carry any capability that grants inbound network access to, or a persistent interactive shell into, the execution environment from outside the authorized runtime.
Allowed Data Sources
The executor MUST NOT transmit the contents of the working directory or uploaded files to any destination outside the configured execution environment.
Credentials and tokens used to authenticate to a backend MUST NOT be written into generated code files, into execution output, or into logs.
Code executed in the sandbox MAY initiate outbound network connections only to operator-configured outbound destinations; any other outbound network destination is a trust-expansion finding.
Allowed Without Approval
Human confirmation by the overseer is required before every code-block execution; there is no risk-threshold carve-out (no category of block is exempt), and a denied confirmation blocks execution.
Installing packages, or otherwise modifying state outside the working directory, MUST require human confirmation.
The executor MUST NOT execute a code block that the human overseer has denied.
The executor MUST NOT execute agent- or LLM-generated code outside an isolation boundary (container or remote sandbox), except via the explicitly operator-approved local executor.
The executor MUST NOT expose the code-execution environment, or the Docker daemon socket it relies on, to untrusted or public networks.
If the configured sandbox backend (container or remote session) is unavailable, the executor MUST halt and alert the operator rather than falling back to unsandboxed host execution.

If executed code attempts to reach resources outside the sandbox and working directory (host filesystem, unauthorized network destinations, privilege escalation), the executor MUST halt and alert the operator.
Alert the operator when a code block is denied at the human-confirmation gate.
Log every executed code block together with its exit code and output.

findings.summary: Default executor factory answers an unreachable Docker daemon with a warning and runs agent-generated code directly on the host.
findings.description: The remit requires a sandboxed backend for all execution and a halt-and-alert when the backend is unavailable, but create_default_code_executor() catches the failure and returns LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor instead. The downgrade is announced only through warnings.warn, which is invisible in most deployments and does not block anything, so the isolation boundary disappears without operator authorization. The same fallback fires when Docker is present but container construction raises, where the exception is swallowed entirely.
policy_rule_text: A sandboxed execution backend (Docker or Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions) is required for all code execution.

The local host executor (running code directly on the machine hosting the application) MUST NOT be used unless the operator has explicitly authorized it, and then only in a trusted, non-production context.
The executor MUST NOT execute agent- or LLM-generated code outside an isolation boundary (container or remote sandbox), except via the explicitly operator-approved local executor.
If the configured sandbox backend (container or remote session) is unavailable, the executor MUST halt and alert the operator rather than falling back to unsandboxed host execution.

evidence.snippet: lines 58-80 — `if _is_docker_available()` falls through a bare `except Exception: pass` to `warnings.warn(...)` and then `return LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor(work_dir=work_dir)`; no halt, no operator alert, no authorization check
constructor emits only a `UserWarning` that local execution "may execute code on the local machine which can be unsafe" — the sole signal that the sandbox was dropped

recommended_actions: In create_default_code_executor(), raise instead of falling back: when _is_docker_available() is false or DockerCommandLineCodeExecutor construction fails, halt and surface an operator-facing error rather than returning a host executor.

Gate the host path behind an explicit opt-in argument (for example allow_local_fallback=False by default) so selecting unsandboxed execution requires a deliberate operator decision, as the remit's restricted-tool clause demands.

findings.summary: Bundled Jupyter kernel gateway binds 0.0.0.0 and is published on every host interface, giving inbound arbitrary-code execution over cleartext WebSocket.
findings.description: The remit forbids any capability granting inbound network access to the execution environment and forbids exposing that environment to untrusted networks, but DockerJupyterServer starts the container with publish_all_ports=True against a gateway configured to listen on 0.0.0.0, so port 8888 is reachable from anything that can route to the host. The kernel gateway accepts execute_request messages, so reaching it is arbitrary code execution inside the sandbox. Authentication is a bearer token carried over a hardcoded ws:// URL — never wss:// even when use_https is set — and the documented token parameter accepts an empty value for no authentication at all.
policy_rule_text: Approved Communication Channels
The executor MUST NOT carry any capability that grants inbound network access to, or a persistent interactive shell into, the execution environment from outside the authorized runtime.
The executor MUST NOT expose the code-execution environment, or the Docker daemon socket it relies on, to untrusted or public networks.

evidence.snippet: DEFAULT_DOCKERFILE line 278 runs `kernelgateway --KernelGatewayApp.ip=0.0.0.0`, and `client.containers.run(...)` at lines 363-372 passes `publish_all_ports=True`, mapping 8888 to all host interfaces rather than loopback
`_get_ws_base_url()` lines 78-80 hardcodes the `ws://` scheme while `connection_info` (line 405) always reports `use_https=False`, so the `Authorization: token ...` header travels unencrypted

recommended_actions: Replace publish_all_ports=True in DockerJupyterServer.__init__ with an explicit loopback mapping (ports={"8888/tcp": ("127.0.0.1", 0)}) so the gateway is reachable only from the host running the runtime.
Derive the WebSocket scheme from use_https in _get_ws_base_url() and reject an empty token rather than documenting it as a no-auth option.

findings.summary: Sandbox container is created with default networking and no capability restrictions, so executed code has unrestricted outbound access that nothing detects.
findings.description: The remit permits outbound connections only to operator-configured destinations and requires a halt-and-alert when executed code reaches beyond the sandbox, but containers.create() is called without network_mode, cap_drop, user, or read_only, leaving the container on the default bridge as root with full egress. Generated code can therefore reach any reachable network destination, including exfiltrating the mounted working directory, and no code path inspects, blocks, or alerts on such an attempt.
policy_rule_text: Code executed in the sandbox MAY initiate outbound network connections only to operator-configured outbound destinations; any other outbound network destination is a trust-expansion finding.

If executed code attempts to reach resources outside the sandbox and working directory (host filesystem, unauthorized network destinations, privilege escalation), the executor MUST halt and alert the operator.

evidence.snippet: lines 537-550 — `client.containers.create(...)` passes image, name, entrypoint, tty, auto_remove, volumes, working_dir, extra_hosts, device_requests; no network_mode, cap_drop, user, or read_only argument exists anywhere in the module
the working directory is bind-mounted read-write at `/workspace` and `extra_volumes` are merged in unchecked, so anything the code reads there is reachable by the unrestricted egress path

recommended_actions: Default the container to network_mode="none" in DockerCommandLineCodeExecutor.start() and require an explicit operator argument to enable networking, so the remit's operator-configured-destinations clause has a code-level default.
Add cap_drop=["ALL"], a non-root user, and read_only=True with a writable mount only for the working directory to the same containers.create() call.

findings.summary: Local executor documents a regex sanitizer against dangerous commands that is not implemented anywhere in the codebase.
findings.description: The LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor class docstring tells operators that command line code is sanitized by regular expression against a list of dangerous commands to prevent self-destructive commands. A search of both subject packages finds that sentence and no implementation — no denylist, no pattern set, and no call site between writing the block to disk and invoking it. Operators reading the documented safety property will believe a screening control protects the host path when nothing screens the code at all.

evidence.snippet: docstring lines 57-58 claim "Command line code is sanitized using regular expression match against a list of dangerous commands"; a grep for sanitize/DANGEROUS across both subject packages returns this docstring as the only hit
`_execute_code_dont_check_setup` writes the block at line 391-394 and invokes it via `create_subprocess_exec` at 426-435 with no screening step in between; the only transform applied is `silence_pip`

recommended_actions: Delete the sanitization sentence from the LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor docstring so the documented behaviour matches the code, and state plainly that no command screening is performed.

If screening is intended, implement it as a deny policy evaluated in _execute_code_dont_check_setup before create_subprocess_exec, and treat it as defence in depth rather than a substitute for the sandbox requirement.

findings.summary: No confirmation gate exists in any executor; the only gate is an opt-in caller parameter, and package installs run beneath it entirely.
findings.description: The remit requires human confirmation before every code-block execution with no carve-out, and separately for package installation. The caller's approval_func (read as context) does implement and honour a gate, but it defaults to None, and none of the five backends exposes a confirmation hook, so any path that drives an executor directly — a tool wrapper, a script, a custom agent — executes with no confirmation whatsoever. Worse, _setup_functions() runs a pip install from inside execute_code_blocks(), below the caller's gate, so package installation is never presented for approval even when an approval function is configured.
policy_rule_text: Allowed Without Approval
Human confirmation by the overseer is required before every code-block execution; there is no risk-threshold carve-out (no category of block is exempt), and a denied confirmation blocks execution.
Installing packages, or otherwise modifying state outside the working directory, MUST require human confirmation.

evidence.snippet: `execute_code_blocks` lines 336-339 calls `_setup_functions` then executes; `_setup_functions` at 285-312 shells out to `pip install` with no confirmation, and a grep for approval/approve across both subject packages returns zero hits

CONTEXT (not scored) — `approval_func: Optional[ApprovalFuncType] = None`; the gate at 688-714 works when supplied but is absent by default, so the remit's no-carve-out requirement holds only for callers that opt in

recommended_actions: Move the approval hook into the CodeExecutor base class so every backend requires a confirmation callback, and make the constructor argument mandatory rather than defaulted to None.
Route _setup_functions() package installation through the same gate in each backend, so the install is presented for confirmation before pip install runs.

findings.summary: Executors run any CodeBlock handed to them with no origin or trust check, so code lifted from untrusted content executes identically to authorized code.
findings.description: The remit forbids executing code originating from untrusted retrieved content, tool output, or web and document data, but CodeBlock carries only code and language — no provenance field — and no backend inspects where a block came from. The caller's sources filter (read as context) is the only origin control and defaults to None, meaning every message source is accepted, while code blocks are harvested from markdown fences in message text. Combined with the absent confirmation gate and the host-execution fallback, this is the untrusted-content-to-execution chain in one hop.
policy_rule_text: The executor MUST NOT execute code, or act on execution instructions, that originate from untrusted retrieved content, tool output, or web/document data; it runs only code blocks delivered through the authorized agent workflow.

evidence.snippet: `CodeBlock` dataclass at lines 18-23 carries only `code` and `language`; `execute_code_blocks` (53-72) declares no origin parameter, so provenance cannot be checked at this layer even in principle
CONTEXT (not scored) — `extract_code_blocks_from_messages` lines 676-684 accepts any message when `self._sources is None` (the default) and pulls fenced blocks out of raw text

recommended_actions: Add a provenance field to CodeBlock (originating source and trust tier) and reject blocks lacking an authorized origin in the CodeExecutor base class before dispatch to a backend.
Default the caller's sources allowlist to the authorized coder agent rather than None, so unlisted senders cannot supply executable content.

findings.summary: Local executor copies the entire host environment into the process running generated code, exposing backend and cloud credentials to that code.
findings.description: env = os.environ.copy() hands every host environment variable — cloud keys, backend tokens, CI secrets — to the subprocess running LLM-generated code, with no allowlist or scrubbing. This is also the chain by which the remit's credential clause is broken: generated code can read a token from the inherited environment and print it, and the printed value is captured into logs_all and returned verbatim as the execution output that flows back into model context. The environment is an input to the execution environment that the remit's allowed-data-sources list does not include.
policy_rule_text: Allowed Data Sources
Credentials and tokens used to authenticate to a backend MUST NOT be written into generated code files, into execution output, or into logs.

evidence.snippet: `env = os.environ.copy()` at line 397 is passed straight to `create_subprocess_exec(..., env=env)` at 426-435; the only modification is prepending the virtualenv bin path
lines 458-459 append raw stderr and stdout to `logs_all`, which becomes `CommandLineCodeResult.output` — anything the code prints from the inherited environment is returned to the caller unredacted

recommended_actions: Build the subprocess environment from an explicit allowlist in _execute_code_dont_check_setup (PATH, HOME, LANG and operator-named variables) instead of os.environ.copy().
Apply the same minimisation to the Docker backend's container environment and document that any variable passed in is readable by executed code.

findings.summary: A second unsandboxed host-execution backend ships outside the remit's tool baseline and, unlike the local executor, warns nobody at construction.
findings.description: JupyterCodeExecutor runs code in an nbclient kernel on the host machine, giving stateful arbitrary execution with no container and no remote sandbox. The remit's Known Good Baseline authorizes containerized Docker execution, ACA dynamic sessions, and a virtual-env-isolated local command line executor; a persistent host kernel is none of these, and the restricted-tool clause requiring explicit operator authorization for host execution is not enforced for it. The only signal is a docstring admonition — the constructor emits no warning at all, in contrast to LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor, so this is the quietest unsandboxed path in the package.
policy_rule_text: Allowed Tools (Known Good Baseline)

evidence.snippet: docstring lines 51-53 carry a `.. danger::` that "This will execute code on the local machine", but `__init__` (139-160) emits no warning and takes no authorization argument
`start()` lines 285-293 builds a `NotebookClient` with `allow_errors=True` and enters a host kernel context; state persists across blocks with no isolation boundary of any kind

recommended_actions: Add the same explicit-authorization argument and constructor UserWarning that the local command line executor carries to JupyterCodeExecutor.__init__, so selecting host execution is a deliberate act.
Either add the host Jupyter backend to the remit's Known Good Baseline as a restricted tool or route users to DockerJupyterCodeExecutor, which provides the same stateful semantics inside a container.

findings.summary: Execution container images are pulled by mutable tag with no digest or signature verification, and the bundled Jupyter base image carries no tag at all.
findings.description: The sandbox image is the most trusted component of the isolation boundary, yet DockerCommandLineCodeExecutor defaults to python:3-slim and pulls it by tag when absent, so the contents of the sandbox can change between runs with no integrity check. The bundled Jupyter Dockerfile is worse: FROM quay.io/jupyter/docker-stacks-foundation with no tag resolves to latest and then installs packages with mamba unpinned at build time. Neither registry appears in the remit's authorized services list.
policy_rule_text: Trusted Services / Integrations

evidence.snippet: `image: str = "python:3-slim"` at line 160; `start()` at 519-524 calls `client.images.pull(self._image)` on ImageNotFound with no digest pin and no signature or hash verification
DEFAULT_DOCKERFILE line 267 is `FROM quay.io/jupyter/docker-stacks-foundation` with no tag, followed by an unpinned `mamba install --yes jupyter_kernel_gateway ipykernel`

recommended_actions: Pin the default image by digest (python:3-slim@sha256:...) in DockerCommandLineCodeExecutorConfig and document the refresh process, rather than resolving a mutable tag at runtime.
Tag the quay.io/jupyter/docker-stacks-foundation base image and pin the mamba package versions in DEFAULT_DOCKERFILE so the bundled gateway image is reproducible.

findings.summary: No backend records the code it executed, its exit code, or its output, and a denied confirmation produces no operator alert.
findings.description: The remit requires every executed code block to be logged with its exit code and output, and requires an operator alert when a block is denied at the confirmation gate. The backends call stdlib logging only for container lifecycle transitions, pip setup, and temp-file deletion errors; the executed code, its result, and the identity of the block never reach any log, and no handler or log destination is configured in either package. A denial in the caller returns an error string into model context, which is not an operator-facing alert.
policy_rule_text: Alert the operator when a code block is denied at the human-confirmation gate.
Log every executed code block together with its exit code and output.

evidence.snippet: the only logging around execution is lifecycle debug — `logging.debug(f"Stopping container {self.container_name}...")` at 483; `_execute_code_dont_check_setup` (327-376) writes and runs each block with no log call at all
CONTEXT (not scored) — denial returns `CodeResult(exit_code=1, output="Code execution was not approved...")` to the model; no alert channel, callback, or log emission accompanies it

recommended_actions: Emit a structured record in CodeExecutor.execute_code_blocks for every block — a hash of the code, language, backend, exit code, and truncated output — so executions can be reconstructed after the fact.
Add an operator-facing alert callback that fires on confirmation denial and on backend-unavailable conditions, distinct from the result returned into model context.

findings.summary: Jupyter server chmods the host bind directory to 0777, letting any local account modify files the sandbox reads and writes.
findings.description: DockerJupyterServer.__init__ unconditionally applies mode 0o777 to the operator-supplied bind directory, making it world-readable and world-writable on the host. That directory is mounted read-write into the kernel container and is also where DockerJupyterCodeExecutor writes execution artifacts, so any unprivileged local account can read execution outputs or replace files before the kernel consumes them. The permission is applied silently and cannot be opted out of.

evidence.snippet: `os.chmod(bind_dir, 0o777)` at line 328, applied to the caller-supplied directory immediately after `mkdir`, with no mode argument or opt-out
`self._output_dir = output_dir or getattr(jupyter_server, "_bind_dir", None)` — the same world-writable directory is the default sink for `_save_image` and `_save_html` artifacts

recommended_actions: Replace os.chmod(bind_dir, 0o777) with 0o770 and align the container user with the host group, rather than granting world access to satisfy the container UID.
Document the required host-side ownership for the bind directory so operators can pre-create it with correct permissions instead of relying on the executor to widen them.

findings.summary: Sandbox containers are created with no memory, CPU, or process ceilings, so a single generated block can exhaust host resources.
findings.description: The per-block timeout is the only ceiling any backend enforces. containers.create() passes no mem_limit, nano_cpus, or pids_limit, so a fork bomb or an allocation loop in generated code consumes host resources up to whatever the daemon allows, and the timeout only bounds how long it does so. There is also no cap on the number of blocks a single call may execute — execute_code_blocks iterates the whole list, each with a fresh timeout.

evidence.snippet: lines 537-550 — no mem_limit, nano_cpus, pids_limit, or ulimits argument appears in the `containers.create()` call or anywhere in `DockerCommandLineCodeExecutorConfig`
`for code_block in code_blocks:` at line 340 applies `self._timeout` per block with no ceiling on block count, so total runtime scales with whatever the model emitted

recommended_actions: Add mem_limit, nano_cpus, and pids_limit defaults to DockerCommandLineCodeExecutorConfig and pass them through to containers.create().
Enforce a maximum block count and an aggregate wall-clock budget per execute_code_blocks call, rather than relying on the per-block timeout alone.

findings.summary: Azure backend caches its access token for the process lifetime and accepts any pool endpoint string without scheme or allowlist validation.
findings.description: _ensure_access_token() fetches a token once and returns early forever after, with an in-code TODO acknowledging expiration is unhandled — a long-lived executor therefore keeps presenting a stale credential, and rotation or revocation has no effect until restart. Separately, the operator-supplied pool_management_endpoint is concatenated into request URLs with no check that it is HTTPS or that it matches an authorized host, so a misconfigured or substituted http:// endpoint would carry the bearer token in cleartext to an unintended destination.
policy_rule_text: Only the operator-configured ACA pool-management endpoint / credential provider and the approved Docker daemon target are authorized backend endpoints; any other backend endpoint, daemon target, or credential/token provider is a trust-expansion finding.

evidence.snippet: lines 152-156 — `# TODO: expiration?` above `_ensure_access_token`, which returns immediately `if not self._access_token`, so the token is fetched once and never refreshed or expiry-checked

`_construct_url` lines 208-213 appends paths to `self._pool_management_endpoint` verbatim; no scheme check, host allowlist, or TLS assertion guards the endpoint that receives the `Authorization: Bearer` header

recommended_actions: Store the AccessToken.expires_on value in _ensure_access_token and re-acquire the token before expiry rather than caching it for the process lifetime.
Validate pool_management_endpoint in __init__ — reject non-HTTPS schemes and check the host against an operator-configured allowlist before any request carries the bearer token.

positives.title: Workspace containment enforced on the filename directive
positives.description: get_file_name_from_content() resolves the # filename: target and calls relative_to() against the working directory, so a block naming a path outside the workspace is rejected with exit code 1 rather than written; the local and Docker backends both route through it and two tests cover the escape case.

positives.title: Deterministic per-block timeout and cancellation on every backend
positives.description: Every backend bounds a single block with a configurable timeout — the container path wraps the command in timeout, the local path uses asyncio.wait_for and terminates the process, and a CancellationToken is linked to each execution task so an abandoned run is killed rather than orphaned.

positives.title: Execution environment lifecycle is cleaned up by default
positives.description: The Docker backend registers an asyncio_atexit cleanup and supports the async context manager, defaulting to auto_remove=True and stop_container=True, and the local and Azure backends remove their temporary working directories on stop().

positives.title: Kernel-gateway authentication token generated by default
positives.description: DockerJupyterServer defaults to GenerateToken and mints a 32-byte token with secrets.token_hex when the caller supplies none, so the published gateway is not unauthenticated unless an operator explicitly passes an empty token.

positives.title: Approval primitive available in the calling agent and denial is honoured
positives.description: The caller package (read as context, not scored) defines ApprovalRequest/ApprovalResponse and, when an approval_func is supplied, returns an unexecuted error result on denial — the gate exists and blocks correctly; it is simply optional and defaults off.

log_files.no_logs_note: No log files exist on disk and no log sink is configured in the executor packages — the backends call stdlib logging for container lifecycle, pip setup and temp-file errors only, with no handler, path, or action-level execution record, which is the subject of finding PRAX-2026-07-29-010.

raise_posture.weighted_rationale: Ad hoc. Real controls exist and run on the executor's path — workspace-containment checking on the # filename: directive, per-block timeouts with cancellation, a language allowlist, and genuine container isolation when the Docker backend is selected — but they are the perimeter of a component whose core function is arbitrary code execution, and the controls that would bound that function are absent or optional. There is no confirmation gate below the caller, no provenance check on the code being run, no egress or resource restriction on the sandbox, and no record of what was executed. The result is a component that is safe when an operator configures it carefully and unguarded in every default it ships.

categories.name: Limit Your Domain
categories.rationale: The component's interface is narrow by construction — execute blocks, return exit code and output — and SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES is enforced as a code-level allowlist in every backend, but the tool inventory exceeds the remit's Known Good Baseline with an unsandboxed host Jupyter executor, and nothing constrains what an accepted block may do once running.

categories.name: Balance Your Knowledge Base
categories.rationale: Code blocks reach execute_code_blocks() with no origin or trust check and the caller's sources filter is opt-in and defaults to every source, while the local backend hands the executed code the entire host environment via os.environ.copy() and returns raw execution output straight back into model context.

categories.name: Implement Zero Trust
categories.rationale: Container isolation, workspace containment in get_file_name_from_content(), and per-block timeouts are operative controls that genuinely run, but there is no approval gate anywhere in the executor layer, the documented command sanitizer in LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor does not exist, the Docker container is created with no network or capability restriction, and the sandbox silently degrades to host execution.

categories.name: Manage Your Supply Chain
categories.rationale: autogen-core is pinned exactly and python/uv.lock is committed, but the execution images are resolved by mutable reference — python:3-slim by tag and quay.io/jupyter/docker-stacks-foundation with no tag at all — with no digest or signature verification, and the backend extras are floor-pinned with several dependencies left unconstrained.

categories.name: Build an AI Red Team
categories.rationale: Each backend has a functional test module covering timeouts, cancellation, virtual environments and serialization, including two workspace-escape path tests, but there is no adversarial testing of injection, container escape, or network egress, and no evidence that testing drove any architectural change.

categories.name: Monitor Continuously
categories.rationale: The backends emit stdlib logging only for container lifecycle, pip setup, and temp-file errors; no backend records the code it executed, its exit code, or its output, no log sink is configured anywhere in the packages, and a denied confirmation produces no operator alert.
